nationality_or_literary_tradition: Irish; poet, critic and teacher writing in English
literary_identity: Irish poet and critic who made the domestic life of women in the suburbs a subject of Irish poetry, and whose later work brought the silence of women into the national history
biography: Eavan Aisling Boland was born in Dublin on 24 September 1944, the daughter of the diplomat Frederick Boland and the painter Frances Kelly. Her father's postings took the family to London in 1950, where she met the anti-Irish hostility she later recorded in 'An Irish Childhood in England: 1951', and then to New York; she returned to Dublin at fourteen to attend the Holy Child School, Killiney, and read English at Trinity College Dublin, graduating in 1966. Her first pamphlet, 23 Poems, appeared in 1962; New Territory (1967), The War Horse (1975), In Her Own Image (1980), Night Feed (1982), The Journey (1987), Outside History (1990), In a Time of Violence (1994), The Lost Land (1998), Code (2001), Against Love Poetry (2001) and Domestic Violence (2007) followed, with the prose study Object Lessons (1995) and A Journey with Two Maps (2011). She taught at Stanford University from 1996 and was a regular reviewer and broadcaster; she died in Dublin on 27 April 2020.
literary_profile: Poetry: 23 Poems (1962), New Territory (1967), The War Horse (1975), In Her Own Image (1980), Night Feed (1982), The Journey (1987), Selected Poems (1989), Outside History (1990), In a Time of Violence (1994), The Lost Land (1998), Code (2001), Against Love Poetry (2001), Domestic Violence (2007), New Collected Poems (2008) and The Historians (2020). Prose: Object Lessons: The Life of the Woman and the Poet in Our Time (1995) and A Journey with Two Maps: Becoming a Woman Poet (2011).
stylistic_characteristics: Conversational, plain and exact free verse, with short lines and unemphatic enjambment; a rhetoric of questions and direct address; the lyric 'I' placed in kitchens, gardens, hospitals and suburban streets; later poems built of compressed, epigrammatic stanzas and of a deliberately bare diction that refuses the ornament of the Irish poetic tradition.
intellectual_concerns: The lives of women in the Irish suburbs, marriage, motherhood and domestic work; the silence of women in official Irish history and in the literary tradition; the Famine, the emigrant ship and the ''hidden' past; language and naming, especially the English of the colonised; a woman poet's relation to the Irish poetic inheritance from Yeats and the Revival.
historical_significance: Boland is the central Irish woman poet of her generation and one of the most influential poets in Ireland in the last fifty years; her insistence that the domestic and the suburban were proper subjects for Irish poetry changed the terms of the tradition, and her work as editor, teacher and critic (Object Lessons) helped make the case for a woman's tradition in Irish writing.
bibliographical_notes: The titles and dates above come from Wikipedia's article on Boland, read directly, from the contents listing of New Collected Poems in a library catalogue, and from general knowledge; they were not checked against a bibliography. Installment 10 records only the three Norton selections, 'Fond Memory' (The Journey, 1987), 'The Dolls Museum in Dublin' (In a Time of Violence, 1994) and 'The Lost Land' (The Lost Land, 1998); the other collections have no records, so the bibliography is incomplete.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Canadian; poet, classicist, translator and essayist writing in English
literary_identity: Canadian poet and classicist whose genre-breaking books - verse essays, translations of Sappho and Greek tragedy, and the novel-in-verse Autobiography of Red - made her one of the most original poets in English of her generation
biography: Anne Patricia Carson was born in Toronto on 21 June 1950 and grew up in a series of small Ontario towns, the daughter of a bank manager. She read classics at the University of Toronto (BA 1974), took an MA there and a PhD in classics at the University of Toronto in 1981, and taught classics and creative writing at the universities of Calgary, Princeton, Emory, McGill, Michigan and New York University. Her first books were academic - Eros the Bittersweet (1986), a study of desire in Sappho and the Greek lyric poets - and her poetry began with Short Talks (1992) and Plainwater (1995), followed by Glass, Irony and God (1995), Autobiography of Red (1998), Men in the Off Hours (2000), The Beauty of the Husband (2001), Decreation (2005), Nox (2010), Antigonick (2012), Red Doc> (2013), Float (2016) and Wrong Norma (2024), with translations of Sappho (If Not, Winter, 2002), Euripides (Bakkhai, 2015) and others. She has won the Lannan Literary Award, a MacArthur Fellowship, the Griffin Poetry Prize (twice), the T. S. Eliot Prize and the Princess of Asturias Award, and was appointed a Member of the Order of Canada in 2005.
literary_profile: Poetry and verse prose: Short Talks (1992), Plainwater (1995), Glass, Irony and God (1995), Autobiography of Red (1998), Men in the Off Hours (2000), The Beauty of the Husband (2001), Decreation (2005), Nox (2010), Antigonick (2012), Red Doc> (2013), Float (2016) and Wrong Norma (2024). Criticism and essays: Eros the Bittersweet (1986) and The Albertine Workout (2014). Translations: If Not, Winter: Fragments of Sappho (2002), Grief Lessons: Four Plays by Euripides (2006), An Oresteia (2009) and Bakkhai (2015).
stylistic_characteristics: A spare, epigrammatic, often flatly declarative free verse, with line breaks used as a form of argument; the collage of poetry, prose, quotation, translation and scholarly footnote; a tone of deadpan wit and sudden emotional exposure; long sequences built of short numbered sections.
intellectual_concerns: Desire, eros and the body; the classical tradition and its modern uses; translation and the fragment; siblings, marriage and the family romance; grief, absence and the failure of language; the essay as a poetic form and the poem as a form of thinking.
historical_significance: Carson is the most formally inventive poet in English of her generation and the one who has done most to reopen the border between poetry, translation and the essay; her Sappho translations and her verse novel Autobiography of Red are standard points of reference in the study of contemporary poetry, and the Nobel Prize in 2026 confirmed a reputation long established among poets and critics.
bibliographical_notes: The titles and dates above come from Wikipedia's article on Carson, read directly, and from general knowledge; they were not checked against a bibliography. Installment 10 records only the Norton selection, 'The Glass Essay' (Glass, Irony and God, 1995), printed as an extract; the other collections, the translations and the criticism have no records, so the bibliography is incomplete.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Northern Irish and Irish; poet, critic and editor writing in English
literary_identity: Northern Irish poet whose formal virtuosity, sly wordplay and long sequences of oblique narrative made him the most influential Irish poet of the generation after Heaney
biography: Paul Muldoon was born on 20 June 1951 on a farm at The Moy, near Portadown in County Armagh, the eldest of three children of a farmer and a schoolteacher, and was educated at Queen's University Belfast, where he read English and came under the influence of Seamus Heaney and the Belfast Group. New Weather (1973) appeared while he was still a student; Mules (1977), Why Brownlee Left (1980), Quoof (1983), Meeting the British (1987), Madoc: A Mystery (1990), The Annals of Chile (1994, T. S. Eliot Prize), Hay (1998), Moy Sand and Gravel (2002, Pulitzer Prize), Horse Latitudes (2006), Maggot (2010), One Thousand Things Worth Knowing (2015) and Howdie-Skelp (2021) followed, with the critical collection To Ireland, I (2000) and the libretti and song cycles written with Warren Zanes and others. He worked as an arts producer for the BBC in Belfast from 1973 to 1986 and has taught at the University of East Anglia, Cambridge and Princeton, where he is Howard G. B. Clark '21 University Professor in the Humanities; he was Oxford Professor of Poetry from 1999 to 2004 and poetry editor of The New Yorker from 2007 to 2017.
literary_profile: Poetry: New Weather (1973), Mules (1977), Why Brownlee Left (1980), Quoof (1983), Meeting the British (1987), Madoc: A Mystery (1990), The Annals of Chile (1994), Hay (1998), Moy Sand and Gravel (2002), Horse Latitudes (2006), Maggot (2010), One Thousand Things Worth Knowing (2015) and Howdie-Skelp (2021); Selected Poems 1968-1986 (1986) and Poems 1968-1998 (2001). Criticism: To Ireland, I (2000).
stylistic_characteristics: Extravagant, punning, syntactically dislocated verse that moves between strict traditional forms - sonnet, sestina, villanelle, haiku - and free verse; dense internal rhyme and assonance; long sequences of short sections in the voices of other people; a diction that mixes Ulster speech, literary allusion and obscure vocabulary.
intellectual_concerns: Northern Ireland, the Troubles and the inheritance of Irish history; language, translation and the untranslatability of experience; family, parents and the farm; the relation of art to politics and of the poet to his predecessors; exile, America and the crossing of borders.
historical_significance: Muldoon has been the dominant formal presence in Irish poetry since the 1980s, and his influence on younger poets in Ireland, Britain and America has been decisive; the Pulitzer Prize and the T. S. Eliot Prize, together with his long tenure as The New Yorker's poetry editor, made him the most publicly prominent Irish poet of his generation after Heaney.
bibliographical_notes: The titles and dates above come from Wikipedia's article on Muldoon, read directly, and from general knowledge; they were not checked against a bibliography. Installment 10 records only the Norton selections - 'Anseo', 'Meeting the British' and '7, Middagh Street' (Meeting the British, 1987) and 'Milkweed and Monarch' (The Annals of Chile, 1994) - and 'Turtles' was dated out of the period (Horse Latitudes, 2006). The later collections have no records, so the bibliography is incomplete.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Canadian; poet, sound poet, editor and children's writer working in English
literary_identity: Canadian poet and sound poet, the central figure of the Toronto concrete and sound poetry scene, whose lifelong poem The Martyrology and early computer poems made language itself the subject of his work
biography: Barrie Phillip Nichol, who signed himself bpNichol, was born in Vancouver on 30 September 1944 and died in Toronto on 25 September 1988. He studied at the University of British Columbia and taught in Vancouver schools before moving to Toronto, where he became a central figure of the small-press and sound-poetry movement: he founded Ganglia Press with David Aylward in 1964 and the magazine grOnk in 1967, edited at Coach House Press from 1975, and was a member of the sound-poetry group The Four Horsemen with Rafael Barreto-Rivera, Paul Dutton and Steve McCaffery. His books include Journeying & the Returns (1967), Konfessions of an Elizabethan Fan Dancer (1969), Still Water (1970), The Martyrology (in nine books, 1972-1990), Continental Trance (1978), Selected Organs (1988) and the computer poems First Screening (1984); he won the Governor General's Award for poetry in 1970 and wrote for the children's television series Fraggle Rock and The Raccoons.
literary_profile: Poetry: Journeying & the Returns (1967), Konfessions of an Elizabethan Fan Dancer (1969), Still Water (1970), The Martyrology, Books 1-2 (1972), The Martyrology, Book 3 (1976), The Martyrology, Book 4 (1977), The Martyrology, Book 5 (1982), The Martyrology, Book 6 (1987), Book 7 (1990) and the posthumous Books 8-9; Continental Trance (1978), Selected Organs (1988) and First Screening: Computer Poems (1984, floppy disk). Children's books and television scripts, including Fraggle Rock and The Raccoons.
stylistic_characteristics: Concrete and visual poetry that treats the page as a field; typewriter poems, hand-drawn letterforms, sound-poetry scores and performance texts; short lyric poems of great simplicity set against the proliferation of The Martyrology; the computer poems of First Screening, in which letters and words move and mutate on the screen.
intellectual_concerns: Language as material and as a system; the letter as image and as sound; the body in performance; spirituality and the 'saints' of The Martyrology, whose names are made from the letters of ordinary words; the relation of writing to reading and of the book to other media.
historical_significance: bpNichol is the central figure of Canadian concrete and sound poetry and a pioneer of electronic literature: First Screening, made in 1983-84 on an Apple IIe, is among the earliest works of programmed kinetic poetry, and The Martyrology is one of the major long poems in Canadian literature. His selection in the Norton Anthology marks the recognition of Canadian avant-garde writing within the English tradition.
bibliographical_notes: The titles and dates above come from Wikipedia's article on bpNichol, read directly, from the Rhizome account of First Screening and from general knowledge; they were not checked against a bibliography. Installment 10 records only the Norton selection, First Screening (1984), as a whole work; the Martyrology books and the other collections have no records, so the bibliography is incomplete.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; playwright, screenwriter and novelist writing in English
literary_identity: British playwright, screenwriter and novelist of Pakistani descent whose plays and films of the 1980s and 1990s made race, class and sexuality in Thatcher's Britain their central subject
biography: Hanif Kureishi was born on 5 December 1954 in Bromley, Kent, the son of an English mother and a Pakistani father who had come to Britain in 1950, and was educated at Bromley Technical High School, Lancaster University and King's College London, where he read philosophy. He began writing for the theatre at the Royal Court and the Hampstead Theatre in the 1970s; his screenplay for Stephen Frears's My Beautiful Laundrette (1985) was nominated for an Academy Award, and Sammy and Rosie Get Laid (1987) and London Kills Me (1989) followed. His plays include The King and Me (1980), Outskirts (1981), Borderline (1981), Birds of Passage (1983), The Mother Country (1984) and Sleep with Me (1999); his fiction includes The Buddha of Suburbia (1990, Whitbread First Novel Award), The Black Album (1995), Intimacy (1998), Gabriel's Gift (2001), Something to Tell You (2008) and The Last Word (2014), and the story collections Love in a Blue Time (1997), Midnight All Day (1999) and The Body (2003). His memoir Shattered (2024) records the spinal injury that left him paralysed in 2022.
literary_profile: Plays: The King and Me (1980), Outskirts (1981), Borderline (1981), Birds of Passage (1983), The Mother Country (1984) and Sleep with Me (1999). Screenplays: My Beautiful Laundrette (1985), Sammy and Rosie Get Laid (1987) and London Kills Me (1989). Fiction: The Buddha of Suburbia (1990), The Black Album (1995), Love in a Blue Time (1997, stories), Intimacy (1998), Midnight All Day (1999), Gabriel's Gift (2001), The Body (2003), Something to Tell You (2008), The Last Word (2014) and Shattered (2024, memoir).
stylistic_characteristics: A colloquial, fast-moving, comic prose and dialogue with a strong ear for London speech and for mixed registers; short scenes and abrupt shifts of tone; a taste for farce and for bodily comedy set against political argument; screenwriting techniques - cross-cutting, montage, close-up - carried into the fiction.
intellectual_concerns: Race, racism and the British Asian experience; class, money and social mobility under Thatcherism; sexuality and the family; popular culture, pop music and the media; religion, secularism and the rise of Islamic fundamentalism; fathers and sons.
historical_significance: Kureishi is the central British Asian writer of his generation and one of the writers who changed the representation of black and Asian Britain on stage and screen in the 1980s; My Beautiful Laundrette and The Buddha of Suburbia are standard texts in the study of black British writing and of postcolonial London.
bibliographical_notes: The titles and dates above come from Wikipedia's article on Kureishi, read directly, and from general knowledge; they were not checked against a bibliography. Installment 10 records only the Norton selection, 'My Son the Fanatic', a story first published in 1994 and collected in Love in a Blue Time (1997); the plays, films and novels have no records, so the bibliography is incomplete.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Scottish; poet and playwright writing in English
literary_identity: Scottish poet and playwright, the first woman, the first Scot and the first openly gay poet to be Poet Laureate, whose dramatic monologues and love poems made her the most widely read British poet of her generation
biography: Carol Ann Duffy was born in the Gorbals, Glasgow, on 23 December 1955, to a Catholic family of Irish descent, and grew up in Stafford, where her father worked for English Electric. She read philosophy at the University of Liverpool and worked as a free-lance writer from 1985. Her collections are Standing Female Nude (1985), Selling Manhattan (1987, Somerset Maugham Award), The Other Country (1990), Mean Time (1993, Whitbread Poetry Award), Selected Poems (1994), The World's Wife (1999), Feminine Gospels (2002), Rapture (2005, T. S. Eliot Prize), The Bees (2011, Costa Poetry Award) and Sincerity (2018), with the plays Take My Husband (1982), Cavern of Dreams (1984), Little Women, Big Boys (1986), Loss (1986) and Casanova (1990), and the children's books and anthologies. She was appointed Poet Laureate in May 2009, the first woman to hold the post, and served until 2019; she is Professor of Contemporary Poetry at Manchester Metropolitan University.
literary_profile: Poetry: Fleshweathercock (1973), Standing Female Nude (1985), Selling Manhattan (1987), The Other Country (1990), Mean Time (1993), Selected Poems (1994), The World's Wife (1999), Feminine Gospels (2002), New Selected Poems (2004), Rapture (2005), The Bees (2011) and Sincerity (2018). Plays: Take My Husband (1982), Cavern of Dreams (1984), Little Women, Big Boys (1986), Loss (1986) and Casanova (1990).
stylistic_characteristics: Accessible, conversational free verse with a strong rhythmic pulse; the dramatic monologue used to give voice to the unheard - wives, servants, figures from myth and history; wordplay, puns and half-rhymes; short lines and sharp, often shocking images; a diction that moves easily between demotic speech and literary allusion.
intellectual_concerns: Love and desire, especially their painful and unequal forms; gender, power and the objectification of women; class, money and the servant's eye; the retelling of myth, fairy tale and history from a woman's point of view; memory, loss and the passage of time; Scotland, England and the languages of both.
historical_significance: Duffy is the most widely read British poet of her generation and the first woman to be Poet Laureate; her poems are set texts in British schools to a degree unmatched by any contemporary, and The World's Wife has become one of the defining collections of the feminist rewriting of myth.
bibliographical_notes: The titles and dates above come from Wikipedia's article on Duffy, read directly, and from general knowledge; they were not checked against a bibliography. Installment 10 records only the Norton selections - 'Warming Her Pearls' (Selling Manhattan, 1987), 'Valentine' (Mean Time, 1993) and 'Medusa' and 'Mrs Lazarus' (The World's Wife, 1999); the other collections and the plays have no records, so the bibliography is incomplete.

literary_identity: Indian novelist whose comic first novel Hullabaloo in the Guava Orchard and whose Booker-winning The Inheritance of Loss made her the youngest woman to win the prize at the time
biography: Kiran Desai was born in New Delhi on 3 September 1971, the daughter of the novelist Anita Desai. She grew up in Delhi, Punjab and Bombay, where she attended the Cathedral and John Connon School, and left India at fifteen; after a year in England she and her mother moved to the United States, where she studied creative writing at Bennington College, Hollins University and Columbia University. Her first novel, Hullabaloo in the Guava Orchard (1998), won the Betty Trask Award; her second, The Inheritance of Loss (2006), set in the Himalayas during the Gorkhaland agitation, won the Man Booker Prize and the National Book Critics Circle Award, making her the youngest woman to win the Booker at the age of thirty-five. She held a Berlin Prize fellowship at the American Academy in Berlin in 2013, and her third novel, The Loneliness of Sonia and Sunny, appeared in 2025 after a gap of nearly two decades.
literary_profile: Novels: Hullabaloo in the Guava Orchard (1998), The Inheritance of Loss (2006) and The Loneliness of Sonia and Sunny (2025).
stylistic_characteristics: Comic, exuberant, image-rich prose with long lists and sudden lyric turns; a strong sense of place - the small-town orchard, the Himalayan hill station - and an ear for the demotic language of Indian English; a narrative that can move between farce and political violence within a paragraph.
intellectual_concerns: Post-independence India and the failures of the state; religion, credulity and the manufacture of holy men; nature, ecology and the encroachments of development; globalisation, migration and the unequal traffic between India and the West; family, parents and the inheritance of disappointment.
historical_significance: Kiran Desai is among the most significant Indian novelists in English of her generation and the winner of the Booker Prize in 2006, and Hullabaloo in the Guava Orchard established the comic idiom that The Inheritance of Loss deepened into a political one; her selection in the Norton Anthology follows the generation of Roy and Rushdie.
bibliographical_notes: The titles and dates above come from Wikipedia's article on Desai, read directly, and from general knowledge; they were not checked against a bibliography. Installment 10 records only the Norton selection, the extract published as 'The Sermon in the Guava Tree' from Hullabaloo in the Guava Orchard (1998); the other novels have no records, so the bibliography is incomplete.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Russian American; novelist, short-story writer, poet, critic and lepidopterist writing in Russian and English
literary_identity: Russian-born American novelist whose baroque style, unreliable narrators and love of pattern made him one of the central prose artists of the twentieth century, in Russian and then in English
biography: Vladimir Vladimirovich Nabokov was born in Saint Petersburg on 22 April 1899 into a wealthy liberal family, and left Russia with his family in 1919; he read at Trinity College, Cambridge, and lived in Berlin and then Paris as an émigré, writing novels and stories in Russian under the pen name V. Sirin. He came to the United States in 1940, taught Russian and European literature at Wellesley College and, from 1948 to 1959, at Cornell University, working as a research entomologist at the American Museum of Natural History and becoming an American citizen in 1945. Lolita (1955, Olympia Press, Paris) made him famous and controversial; Pnin (1957), Pale Fire (1962) and Ada or Ardor (1969) followed, with the memoirs Speak, Memory (1951) and the translations and commentaries on Pushkin's Eugene Onegin (1964). He settled at the Montreux Palace Hotel in Switzerland in 1961 and died there on 2 July 1977.
literary_profile: Novels in Russian: Mary (1926), King, Queen, Knave (1928), The Defence (1930), Glory (1932), Camera Obscura (1932), Despair (1934), Invitation to a Beheading (1936), The Gift (1937). Novels in English: The Real Life of Sebastian Knight (1941), Bend Sinister (1947), Lolita (1955), Pnin (1957), Pale Fire (1962), Ada or Ardor (1969), Transparent Things (1972) and Look at the Harlequins! (1974). Stories: Nabokov's Dozen (1958), Details of a Sunset (1976) and The Stories of Vladimir Nabokov (1995). Memoir and criticism: Speak, Memory (1951), Notes on Prosody (1964), Eugene Onegin, translated and commented (1964) and Strong Opinions (1973).
stylistic_characteristics: A prose of extreme precision and elaborate patterning, with alliteration, puns, multilingual wordplay and buried acrostics; unreliable or self-dramatising narrators; a habit of addressing the reader directly; sensuous detail used as evidence, and a lyric gift that survives translation from the Russian.
intellectual_concerns: Memory and the lost Russian childhood; exile, émigré poverty and the impostures of identity; the relation between art and cruelty; madness, obsession and the tyranny of the imagination; lepidoptery, chess and pattern-making as images of the novelist's work; America as seen by an astonished outsider.
historical_significance: Nabokov is the most influential prose stylist among the Russian émigrés and one of the defining novelists of the century; Lolita and Pale Fire are standard texts in the study of the unreliable narrator and of postmodern fiction, his Cornell lectures shaped several generations of American writers, and the Nabokovian phrase and the Nabokovian puzzle have become common critical currency.
bibliographical_notes: The titles and dates above come from Wikipedia's article on Nabokov and on 'Signs and Symbols', read directly; they were not checked against a bibliography. Installment 10 records only the Norton selection, 'Signs and Symbols' (The New Yorker, 1948; collected in Nabokov's Dozen, 1958); the novels, the other stories and the criticism have no records, so the bibliography is incomplete.
